HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P)

History:
• 39-year-old male (age not explicitly stated; adult) reports 4-day history of upper-respiratory symptoms.  
• Initial symptoms: sore throat with painful swallowing x 1–2 days, clear/runny nasal discharge progressing to persistent nasal congestion.  
• New symptoms: dry, constant cough since yesterday; night sweats for several nights; generalized fatigue.  
• Intermittent low-grade fever at onset—responsive to self-administered paracetamol and ibuprofen.  
• Exertional dyspnea (“winded” when exercising); no rest dyspnea or chest pain.  
• Associated: intermittent generalized headaches; myalgias/arthralgias past 2 days; mild ↓ appetite, ↑ fluid intake.  
• Denies: ear pain/discharge, visual changes, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, rash, bowel/urinary changes.  
• Similar episodes: none mentioned. Possible exposure from coughing/sneezing coworker.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• Surgical history: not discussed.  
• Medications: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented), Ibuprofen (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Drug allergies: none known.  
• Family history: grandmother – type 2 diabetes; great-grandfather – eczema.  
• Social history: Lives alone; accountant. Occasional cigar use at social/work events; occasional alcohol; no regular smoking. No illicit drug use mentioned.

Physical Examination:
(telehealth – limited visual observation)  
• Patient appears tired but in no acute distress (per video).  
• No reported chest pain, throat swelling, ear discharge, or skin rash.  
• Alert and oriented; able to speak full sentences without obvious dyspnea.  
(Full vitals and in-person exam not performed/not available.)

Impression:
Likely viral upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) / early influenza-like illness.

Management Plan:
• Supportive care: rest, adequate hydration, balanced nutrition.  
• Symptomatic treatment: continue Paracetamol and Ibuprofen as needed for fever, headache, myalgias (patient already using).  
• Recommend 1–2 days off work to recuperate.  
• Education on expected course: most viral URTIs resolve within 7–10 days.  
• Red-flag advice: seek urgent review if high fever returns, breathing worsens, chest pain develops, or symptoms persist beyond one week.  
• Follow-up: routine follow-up next week if not improving, or sooner if red-flag symptoms occur.

Patient Summary:
Adult male with 4-day viral prodrome—sore throat now improving, evolving to congestion, dry cough, night sweats, fatigue, and myalgias—consistent with an uncomplicated viral URTI. Presently stable, no alarming features. Supportive management and safety-net advice provided.

Key Takeaways:
1. Rest, fluids, and continue OTC antipyretics/analgesics.  
2. Take 1–2 days off work; expect gradual improvement over the next week.  
3. Return immediately if fever spikes, breathing becomes difficult, or chest pain occurs.

Next Steps:
• Monitor symptoms at home; reassess via clinic/telehealth if no improvement in 7 days.  
• No routine labs or imaging indicated at this stage.  
• Consider COVID-19 or influenza testing if symptoms worsen or public-health guidance changes.
